proposedTopics.title: 2-D Dynamic Programming
proposedTopics.description: DP over two interacting index axes (two strings, or a grid). Direct extension of 1-D DP's tabulation to a 2-D table.

proposedTopics.title: Grid path counting
proposedTopics.description: dp[r][c] built from dp[r-1][c] and dp[r][c-1] (or their min/sum), tabulated row by row. Recognize: "number of paths / min-cost path through a grid, moving only right/down".

proposedTopics.title: Longest common subsequence
proposedTopics.description: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1 if chars match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]); tabulate both strings' prefixes together — the 2-D generalization of Longest Increasing Subsequence's single-sequence recurrence. Recognize: comparing two sequences for shared structure.

proposedTopics.title: Edit distance
proposedTopics.description: dp[i][j] = min cost to convert prefix i of one string to prefix j of the other, taking the best of insert/delete/replace at each step. Recognize: "minimum operations to transform string A into string B".

proposedTopics.title: 0/1 knapsack
proposedTopics.description: dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items within capacity w, deciding include-or-exclude item i (each item usable once, contrast with unbounded coin change). Recognize: fixed set of items each usable at most once, capacity constraint.

proposedTopics.title: Interval DP
proposedTopics.description: dp[i][j] over a subarray/substring range [i,j], built from smaller sub-intervals by trying every split/last-operation point k inside the range. Tabulate by increasing interval length. Recognize: "best way to combine/remove a contiguous range", matrix-chain-style problems.

proposedTopics.title: Palindromic subsequence DP
proposedTopics.description: dp[i][j] = longest palindromic subsequence/substring within s[i..j], expanding inward from single characters and pairs. Recognize: palindrome-related length/count questions over substrings.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for grid-path DP? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: count-the-ways or min/max-cost of walking a 2-D grid with restricted moves (usually only right/down), each cell's answer depending on the cells above and to the left. Pitfall: mishandling the first row/column — with only-right/down moves there is exactly ONE way into any border cell, so seed them explicitly (or with a padding row/col of the identity value) before the general recurrence, or you undercount.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the row-by-row grid-path tabulation in your language of choice: count distinct right/down paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m x n grid, using a single rolling row.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Keep one array of length n for the current row, initialized to all 1s (the top row: one way to each cell). For each subsequent row, walk left to right doing row[c] += row[c-1] — the untouched row[c] is the value from the row above, row[c-1] is the freshly-updated value from the left. Invariant: after processing row r, row[c] holds the path count to cell (r, c). Answer is row[n-1].

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Unique Paths (Medium) — count distinct paths a robot can take from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m x n grid, moving only right or down.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Every cell's count is the sum of the cell above and the cell to the left; border cells are all 1. (Closed form: it's a single binomial coefficient, but the DP generalizes.)

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Unique Paths II (Medium) — same grid path count, but some cells contain obstacles that cannot be entered.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Same above-plus-left recurrence, but force dp = 0 at any obstacle cell (and stop propagating a blocked start/border), so paths through it are never counted.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Minimum Path Sum (Medium) — find the minimum sum of numbers along a path from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid, moving only right or down.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp above, dp left); the first row/column can only accumulate from one direction.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for LCS-style two-string DP? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: two sequences compared for shared structure — longest common run (not necessarily contiguous), min deletions/insertions to align them, similarity scoring. It is the 2-D gateway pattern. Pitfall: confusing subsequence (order preserved, gaps allowed → this DP) with substring (contiguous → different recurrence), and off-by-one indexing between the length-(m+1)x(n+1) table and the 0-based strings. Related: Shortest Common Supersequence reconstructs from the same table.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the LCS table fill in your language of choice: given two strings, compute the length of their longest common subsequence.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Table of (m+1) x (n+1) with a zero row and zero column. For i, j from 1: if a[i-1] == b[j-1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Invariant: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i chars of a and first j chars of b; answer is dp[m][n].

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Longest Common Subsequence (Medium) — length of the longest subsequence present in both of two given strings.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Match extends the diagonal by 1; a mismatch takes the better of dropping one character from either string.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Delete Operation for Two Strings (Medium) — minimum number of single-character deletions to make two strings equal.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The kept characters form the LCS; answer is (len(a) - LCS) + (len(b) - LCS) — everything not in the common subsequence must be deleted from one side or the other.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for edit-distance DP? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: minimum operations to transform one string into another where the allowed moves are insert, delete, and replace one character (Levenshtein). Pitfall: wrong base row/column — converting a length-i prefix to the empty string costs exactly i (i deletions), so dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j must be seeded, not left at 0. Related: One Edit Distance is the k=1 boundary case (premium; skipped here).

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the edit-distance table fill in your language of choice: given two strings, compute the minimum insert/delete/replace operations to convert one into the other.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Table (m+1) x (n+1) with dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j. For i, j from 1: if a[i-1] == b[j-1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (free match), else dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] delete, dp[i][j-1] insert, dp[i-1][j-1] replace). Answer is dp[m][n].

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Edit Distance (Medium) — minimum number of insert, delete, or replace operations to convert word1 into word2.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: On a character match, carry the diagonal for free; otherwise it's 1 + the cheapest of the three neighboring subproblems (delete, insert, replace).

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for 0/1 knapsack DP? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: a fixed set of items each usable at most once, a capacity/target budget, and a best-value or feasibility question ("can a subset hit exactly this sum"). Contrast with unbounded coin change (items reusable). Pitfall: when compressing to a 1-D capacity array you MUST iterate capacity in REVERSE per item — a forward loop reuses the same item within one pass, silently turning it into the unbounded version. Related: Last Stone Weight II is knapsack on half the total sum.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the 1-D 0/1 knapsack update in your language of choice: given item weights and values and a capacity, compute the max value with each item used at most once.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: One array dp of length capacity+1, dp[0] = 0. For each item, loop w from capacity DOWN to the item's weight: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight] + value). The reverse loop guarantees dp[w - weight] still refers to a state WITHOUT the current item. Invariant: after processing k items, dp[w] is the best value achievable within capacity w using only those k items.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Partition Equal Subset Sum (Medium) — decide whether an array can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: If the total is odd it's impossible; otherwise it's a subset-sum (boolean 0/1 knapsack) asking whether some subset reaches total/2.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Target Sum (Medium) — count the ways to assign + or - to each number so the signed sum equals a target.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The positive-sign subset must sum to (total + target) / 2 (reject if that's non-integer or out of range); then it's counting subsets that hit that sum — a knapsack over counts.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for interval DP? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: the optimum over a contiguous range [i, j] is defined by choosing a split point or a LAST operation k inside the range, with sub-ranges solved independently — combining/removing/merging a contiguous sequence. The recurrence is dp[i][j] = best over k in (i, j) of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + cost(i, k, j), and you must fill by INCREASING interval length (all shorter ranges before the ranges that depend on them). Pitfall: iterating i and j in plain order instead of by length, so dp reads sub-intervals that aren't computed yet; also forgetting to pad with sentinel boundaries. Related: Matrix Chain Multiplication (the classic reference, not on LeetCode) and Minimum Cost to Merge Stones.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Burst Balloons (Hard) — maximize coins from bursting all balloons, where bursting i earns nums[left]*nums[i]*nums[right] with left/right being its current neighbors.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Think of k as the LAST balloon burst in an interval, so its neighbors are the fixed boundaries — dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] + dp[k][j] on padded (value-1) boundaries, filled by increasing length.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for palindromic-substring DP? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: length or count questions about palindromic substrings/subsequences of a single string, where the answer for a range depends on its inner range plus its two endpoints. Pitfall: with the expand-around-center technique, forgetting the EVEN-length centers — you must expand from both single characters (odd centers) and every adjacent pair (even centers), or you miss half the palindromes. Related: Longest Palindromic Subsequence is the same table run as LCS of s with its own reverse.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the expand-around-center scan in your language of choice: given a string, find (or count) its palindromic substrings by growing outward from each center.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: For each index, run an expand helper that takes left and right pointers and, while left >= 0 and right < n and s[left] == s[right], steps both outward. Call it twice per index: once with (i, i) for odd-length centers and once with (i, i+1) for even-length centers. Each successful expansion is one palindrome (track its length/bounds, or increment a counter). 2n-1 centers, O(n^2) total.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Longest Palindromic Substring (Medium) — return the longest contiguous substring of s that is a palindrome.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Expand around all 2n-1 centers (each character and each gap between characters), tracking the widest palindrome's bounds.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Palindromic Substrings (Medium) — count how many contiguous substrings of s are palindromes.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Same expand-around-center scan, but add 1 to the count for every successful outward step (each expansion is one distinct palindromic substring).
